```{r setup, include=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This guide uses a small subset of the bundled lizard data so that the examples
run quickly. For correlated traits, continue to the
[multivariate inference guide](multivariate-inference.html).

## Prepare the tree and traits

```{r prepare-data, purl=FALSE}
library(kfl1ou)
data(lizard.tree, lizard.traits)

keep <- lizard.tree$tip.label[seq_len(12)]
tree <- ape::drop.tip(lizard.tree, setdiff(lizard.tree$tip.label, keep))
Y <- lizard.traits[keep, 1, drop = FALSE]
dat <- adjust_data(tree, Y, quietly = TRUE)
dat$tree.scale
```

`adjust_data()` aligns trait rows to tip labels and orders edges in postorder.
The defaults have three other effects:

- `normalize = TRUE` divides every branch length by the tree height. The tree
  retains that factor, and `original_time_parameters(fit)` converts alpha and
  evolutionary variance rates back to the original time unit. Optima and
  observation-error variances stay in trait units. Use `normalize = FALSE` to
  keep the input time scale from the start.
- `drop.all.missing = TRUE` removes tips with no observed trait values, returning
  the induced subtree. Check `removed.tips`; the output need not have the same
  tip set as the input. For multivariate data, partial missingness is retained.
- `drop.invariant = TRUE` removes invariant columns. Check `removed.traits` and
  use `invariant.tolerance` to control this decision.

Repair is separate from normalization and is disabled by default. If a nearly
ultrametric tree needs bounded repair, request it explicitly:

```{r bounded-repair, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
repaired <- adjust_data(
  tree, Y, normalize = FALSE, repair.tree = TRUE,
  ultrametric.tolerance = 0.01
)
```

Repair fails if it cannot meet the allowed relative total branch-length change.
Review the reported change before using the fitted shift positions. If tips or
traits are removed, subset known observation variances to the retained labels
and columns as well.

## Search and inspect what was searched

```{r shift-search, fig.width=8, fig.height=6, purl=FALSE}
fit <- estimate_shift_configuration(
  dat$tree, dat$Y, criterion = "BIC", max.nShifts = 2,
  search.strategy = "auto"
)
plot(fit)
fit$search.diagnostics
original_time_parameters(fit)
```

`search.strategy = "auto"` enumerates small configuration spaces and otherwise
uses ensemble sparse paths. The other choices force `"exhaustive"`, `"lasso"`,
or `"ensemble"`. An ensemble combines the full-data path with deterministically
seeded subsampled paths. For multivariate sparse paths, `rescale` affects
candidate generation; scores and returned fits remain in the original trait
units. Exhaustive and univariate searches do not use that rescaling.

The search space is bounded by candidate edges, the maximum number of shifts,
and estimability. In particular, unregularized full covariance with n tips and
p traits caps the search at n - p - 1 shifts. Inspect these diagnostics:

| Field in `fit$search.diagnostics` | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `configuration.space.size` | Size of the requested raw configuration space after restrictions. |
| `evaluated.configurations` and `coverage` | Evaluated candidates and coverage within that space; equivalent placements can be collapsed. |
| `globally.optimal` | Whether the discrete search enumerated the admissible space; not a guarantee of global numerical optimization or historical identifiability. |
| `estimability` | Requested/effective shift limit and the reason for any reduction. |
| `ensemble` | Attempted, successful and failed extra paths, with failure messages. Zero attempts are expected for an exhaustive search. |

For a sparse search, model averaging is limited to evaluated candidates. A
large failure count or low search coverage calls for investigation or broader
search, not an interpretation of the best score as certainty.

## Known and estimated observation error

Known `input_error` values are **variances**, not standard deviations. They may
be tip-specific vectors or tip-by-trait matrices. `measurement_error = TRUE`
estimates an additional shared observation variance `sigma2_error` per trait.
The two sources can be used separately or together:

| Input | Covariance contribution |
|---|---|
| `input_error` only | Known tip-specific diagonal variances. |
| `measurement_error = TRUE` only | An estimated variance per trait, shared across tips. |
| Both | Known variances plus the estimated extra variance. |

The following values are illustrative; replace them with measurement-derived
variances for an analysis.

```{r observation-error, purl=FALSE}
known_tip_variances <- matrix(
  0.01, nrow(dat$Y), ncol(dat$Y), dimnames = dimnames(dat$Y)
)
fit_with_error <- estimate_shift_configuration(
  dat$tree, dat$Y, criterion = "BIC", max.nShifts = 1,
  input_error = known_tip_variances, measurement_error = TRUE
)
fit_with_error$sigma2_error
```

For one trait the total covariance is
`Sigma_phylo + Diag(input_error) + sigma2_error I`.
`fit_l1ou_replicates()` instead accepts replicate-by-trait measurements and
species labels, estimates each species mean and its sampling variance, and
propagates that variance as known input error. Its singleton handling is an
explicit modelling choice; inspect the returned replicate summaries.

## Diagnostics and uncertainty

```{r diagnostics, purl=FALSE}
diagnostics <- diagnose_l1ou(fit)
diagnostics[c("convergence", "boundary", "trait.covariance.condition")]
fit$alpha
fit$l1ou.options$alpha.upper

averaged <- model_average_l1ou(fit, delta.max = 10)
utils::head(data.frame(weight = as.numeric(averaged$partition.weights)), 5L)
```

This table shows the five largest weights over canonical tip partitions. The
names in `averaged$partition.weights` identify the corresponding partitions.

Unavailable optimizer diagnostics are `NA`, not evidence of convergence. Check
alpha against its bounds and use `profile_alpha_l1ou()` and
`alpha_to_half_life()` to assess weak identification. `vcov()` returns
coefficient sampling covariance, when available; `evolutionary_vcov()` returns
evolutionary innovation covariance.

The following blocks are intentionally not run during ordinary vignette
builds. Choose an adequate simulation count for scientific inference; the
small counts used by development smoke checks only verify that the code runs.

```{r simulation-count, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
n_replicates <- 200L
```

```{r bootstrap, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
support <- l1ou_bootstrap_support(
  fit, nItrs = n_replicates, type = "parametric", seed = 2,
  multicore = TRUE, nCores = 2
)
support[c("attempted", "successful", "failed", "failure.messages")]
summarize_shift_uncertainty(support, dat$tree)
```

Parametric bootstrap simulates the fitted OU process directly along branches,
including fitted observation error, and repeats the configured shift search.
`type = "residual"` uses the historical whitening and residual-resampling
procedure instead. Both retain trait-specific missingness. Full trait
covariance uses joint cross-trait simulation or whitening, respectively.
Unix-like systems use fork workers and Windows uses socket clusters; nested
model fits respect the total CPU budget.

```{r full-intervals, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
intervals <- confint(
  fit, method = "parametric", selection = "full",
  interval = "basic", nsim = n_replicates, seed = 3
)
intervals
attr(intervals, "failed")
attr(intervals, "failure.messages")
```

`selection = "conditional"` keeps the selected shift and convergence constraints;
`"full"` repeats the stored search, including its shift limit, and repeats
convergence discovery for convergent inputs. If starting from `fit_OU()` rather
than a search result, set `search.max.nShifts` explicitly: its default is at
least one, not an unlimited search. Exact-edge coefficient intervals and tip
partitions answer different questions. Root-complement or other equivalent
edge placements can describe the same partition, so bootstrap summaries and
model averaging also report canonical partitions and tip co-assignment.
Failed refits are omitted; report their counts and messages rather than
silently treating the requested simulation count as the successful count.

For sensitivity to tree topology, `fit_l1ou_tree_ensemble()` fits alternative
trees with the same tip labels and combines results through tip partitions.
Use `sensitivity_l1ou()` for root-model and alpha-bound sensitivity and
`check_rate_heterogeneity()` for simulation-calibrated clade-rate diagnostics.

## Interpretation

Shift configurations describe phylogenetically consistent trait clusters;
extant tips alone generally cannot identify exact historical shift positions,
counts or times. OU optima, rates and observation error can be weakly identified.
Report sensitivity to bounds, root models, information criteria and resampling.
pBIC for unconstrained shifts follows the original l1ou derivation; its extension
to convergent equality constraints remains heuristic. The diagonal-trait pBIC
coefficient determinant is evaluated in OU optimum coordinates at each model's
fitted alpha. Free fits use mean displacements internally, so their covariance
determinant includes the change of coordinates
`mean displacement = (1 - exp(-alpha * parent age)) * optimum change`.
All-singleton convergence groups and the corresponding unconstrained fit thus
have the same pBIC at the same parameters. Fixed alpha contributes no estimated
parameter penalty; shifted exact-zero-alpha models receive infinite pBIC
because their OU optima are unidentifiable.
With known observation variances, the determinant uses the conditional mean
information at the fitted covariance. The usual sample-size adjustment of the
residual-scaled coefficient covariance is insufficient for these models.

Versions through 3.0.12 mixed mean-displacement and optimum coordinates and used
the unconstrained alpha in the convergent determinant. The correction changes
pBIC scores and can change selected models and weights; previous pBIC analyses
must be rerun. It does not establish error calibration of the convergence
extension. BIC and AICc are unaffected.

Convergent models are
refitted under those constraints, so returned coefficients, fitted values,
likelihoods and variance parameters describe the constrained model.
